(Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. ## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

name: Fly Deploy

  push:
    branches:
      - main

      - name: Setup Vite+
        uses: voidzero-dev/setup-vp@v1

      - name: Install dependencies

      - name: Run linting

      - name: Run tests with coverage
        run: vp test run --coverage

      - name: Build application
        run: vp build

  deploy:
    name: Deploy app
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && github.event_name == 'push'
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Flyctl
        uses: superfly/flyctl-actions/setup-flyctl@master

      - name: Deploy to Fly.io
        run: flyctl deploy --remote-only

<!--VITE PLUS START-->

# Using Vite+, the Unified Toolchain for the Web

This project is using Vite+, a unified toolchain built on top of Vite, Rolldown, Vitest, tsdown, Oxlint, Oxfmt, and Vite Task. Vite+ wraps runtime management, package management, and frontend tooling in a single global CLI called `vp`. Vite+ is distinct from Vite, and it invokes Vite through `vp dev` and `vp build`. Run `vp help` to print a list of commands and `vp <command> --help` for information about a specific command.

Docs are local at `node_modules/vite-plus/docs` or online at https://viteplus.dev/guide/.

## Built-in Commands vs Scripts

`vp <name>` runs a built-in command. `vp run <name>` runs a `package.json` script or a `vite.config.ts` task. Scripts cannot overwrite built-ins, so `vp dev` and `vp run dev` may do different things. Check `package.json` and `vite.config.ts` first, and run `vp run <name>` when the project defines a script or task with that name.

## Tool Versions

Run `vp toolchain` to show versions and relationships in the active Vite+
release. Add a tool name to select part of the graph. For example, run
`vp toolchain vite`. Use `--global` to ignore the local `vite-plus` package. Use
`vp why <package>` to show the package-manager dependency graph.

## Review Checklist

- [ ] Run `vp install` after pulling remote changes and before getting started.
- [ ] Run `vp check` and `vp test` to format, lint, type check and test changes.
- [ ] Check if there are `vite.config.ts` tasks or `package.json` scripts necessary for validation, run via `vp run <script>`.
- [ ] If setup, runtime, or package-manager behavior looks wrong, run `vp env doctor` and include its output when asking for help.

<!--VITE PLUS END-->

# Groq Production Models for Low-Latency Chat

Based on the documentation, here are the **small/fast production models** best suited for low-latency chat applications:

## Recommended Options

**OpenAI GPT OSS 20B** (`openai/gpt-oss-20b`)
- Speed: "1000" tokens/second (fastest available)
- Cost: $0.075 input / $0.30 output per 1M tokens
- Context: 131,072 tokens
- Ideal for real-time chat requiring minimal latency

**OpenAI GPT OSS 120B** (`openai/gpt-oss-120b`)
- Speed: "~500 tps"
- More capable but slightly slower than the 20B variant
- Better for complex reasoning within acceptable latency

## Why These Models?

The GPT OSS 20B stands out as the optimal choice for low-latency assistants, delivering "1000" tokens per second—double the speed of larger alternatives. This throughput enables rapid response times while maintaining reasonable quality for most conversational tasks.

The 120B model offers enhanced capabilities when response time constraints are less strict, providing superior reasoning at the cost of approximately 50% latency increase.

I've completed the web search. Here are the key findings about AI SDK 7, streamText, tool calling, and structured output best practices for 2026:

## Key Findings

**Combining streamText with Tool Calling and Structured Output:**

Structured output generation is part of the generateText and streamText flow, meaning you can combine it with tool calling in the same request.

**Best Practices:**

1. **Step Management**: When using output with tool calling, the structured output generation counts as an additional step in the execution flow. When using tools with structured output, remember that generating the structured output counts as a step, and you should configure stopWhen to allow enough steps for both tool execution and output generation.

2. **Schema Specification**: The AI SDK standardizes structured object generation across model providers using the output property on generateText and streamText, with support for Zod schemas, Valibot, or JSON schemas.

3. **Use Cases**: generateText is ideal for non-interactive use cases where you need to write text (e.g. drafting email or summarizing web pages) and for agents that use tools.

4. **Schema Hints**: You can add .describe("...") to individual schema properties to give the model hints about what each property is for, which helps improve the quality and accuracy of generated structured data.

The search results confirm that both `streamText` and `generateText` support tool calling and structured output simultaneously, making them versatile for 2026 AI applications.

# Deployment and Rendering

TanStack Start deploys to any hosting provider via Vite and Nitro. This skill covers hosting setup, SSR configuration, prerendering, and SEO.

## Hosting Providers

### Cloudflare Workers

```bash
pnpm add -D @cloudflare/vite-plugin wrangler
```

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import { tanstackStart } from '@tanstack/react-start/plugin/vite'
import { cloudflare } from '@cloudflare/vite-plugin'
import viteReact from '@vitejs/plugin-react'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    cloudflare({ viteEnvironment: { name: 'ssr' } }),
    tanstackStart(),
    viteReact(),
  ],
})
```

```jsonc
// wrangler.jsonc
{
  "name": "my-app",
  "compatibility_date": "2025-09-02",
  "compatibility_flags": ["nodejs_compat"],
  "main": "@tanstack/react-start/server-entry",
}
```

Deploy: `npx wrangler login && pnpm run deploy`

> **Worker env is per-request.** Cloudflare Workers inject env vars at request time. `process.env.X` at module scope evaluates to `undefined` even on the server. The Cloudflare-canonical way to read env (including from module scope) is the `cloudflare:workers` env binding:
>
> ```ts
> import { env } from 'cloudflare:workers'
> const apiHost = env.API_HOST
> ```
>
> Or read `process.env.X` per-request inside `.handler()` / middleware `.server()`. See [Cloudflare's environment-variables docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/environment-variables/) and [start-core/execution-model](../execution-model/SKILL.md).

### Netlify

```bash
pnpm add -D @netlify/vite-plugin-tanstack-start
```

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import { tanstackStart } from '@tanstack/react-start/plugin/vite'
import netlify from '@netlify/vite-plugin-tanstack-start'
import viteReact from '@vitejs/plugin-react'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [tanstackStart(), netlify(), viteReact()],
})
```

Deploy: `npx netlify deploy`

### Nitro (Vercel, Railway, Node.js, Docker)

```bash
npm install nitro@npm:nitro-nightly@latest
```

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import { tanstackStart } from '@tanstack/react-start/plugin/vite'
import { nitro } from 'nitro/vite'
import viteReact from '@vitejs/plugin-react'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [tanstackStart(), nitro(), viteReact()],
})
```

Build and start: `npm run build && node .output/server/index.mjs`

### Bun

Bun deployment requires React 19. For React 18, use Node.js deployment.

```ts
// vite.config.ts — add bun preset to nitro
plugins: [tanstackStart(), nitro({ preset: 'bun' }), viteReact()]
```

## Selective SSR

content.text:
I dug through the whole codebase, ran the build, the tests, and the type checker, and checked your deps and CI against upstream. Here's what I found.

## The short answer on your actual question

**There are no dependency upgrades to do.** `npm outdated` returns nothing, and spot-checks confirm it (react 19.2.8 is current). Your recent "Updated dependencies" commits did their job.

But dependency currency is exactly what bit you: **two things are broken in production right now, both from upstream changes.**

---

## P0 — Broken today

### 1. The AI command palette is dead

`src/server/ai.functions.ts:135` uses `groq("llama-3.1-8b-instant")`. Groq **shut that model down on August 16, 2026** — five days ago. Their recommended replacement is `openai/gpt-oss-20b`.

Worse, it fails silently: the `catch` at `ai.functions.ts:159` swallows the error into `"AI request failed. Try again."`, so there's no signal anything is wrong.

The fix is one string — I verified `'openai/gpt-oss-20b'` is already in `@ai-sdk/groq`'s `GroqChatModelId` union, so it's a drop-in. It's also faster (~1000 tps vs the old model) and cheap ($0.075/$0.30 per 1M). Two other spots need the same edit: the hardcoded `"llama-3.1"` label at `CommandAgent.tsx:554`, and I'd add a `console.error` + a distinguishable user message so the next shutdown isn't invisible.

### 2. `main` is red — deploys are blocked

Run `32480357913` (commit `9f33fb6`, "Updated dependencies") failed in 31s:

```
Error: vite-plus bundles vitest@4.1.10, but @vitest/coverage-v8@4.1.11 is installed.
```

I reproduced it locally. Your last dependency bump pushed vitest/coverage-v8 to 4.1.11, but `vite-plus@0.2.9` bundles 4.1.10. Three places need to agree: `devDependencies.vitest`, `devDependencies.@vitest/coverage-v8`, and `overrides.vitest` — all to `4.1.10`.

**Heads up before you fix it:** your coverage gate is currently inert and will start biting. `vite.config.ts:59` has `thresholds: { global: { branches: 70, ... } }`. In Vitest 4 the type is `Thresholds | ({[glob: string]: ...} & Thresholds)` — so `global` is parsed as a *glob pattern* matching zero files. The 70% gate has been enforcing nothing. Once coverage runs again with `thresholds: { branches: 70, functions: 70, lines: 70, statements: 70 }` at the top level, it will very likely fail: you have 17 tests covering `utils/` and `ToolCard`, while four route files and the 562-line `CommandAgent` are untested.

While you're in there: `overrides.vite: npm:@voidzero-dev/vite-plus-core@0.2.8` is stale — `npm ls` resolves 0.2.9. Worth confirming it's still load-bearing at all.

---

## P1 — The architectural one

**This should be a static site, and isn't.** Three symptoms, one root cause:

**a) `/blog` ships every post's full HTML.** `fetchAllBlogPosts()` returns `BlogPost[]` including `html`, and the loader hands all of it to the hydration payload. Measured against your production build: **30,005 of the 46,082 bytes of `/blog` (65%) is the hydration payload**, most of it rendered article HTML the list page never displays. This grows linearly with every post you write. Minimum fix: a list DTO that omits `html`.

**b) A server round-trip for build-time-constant data.** The markdown is `import.meta.glob`'d at build time and never changes, yet `/blog` and `/blog/$slug` go through server functions on every client navigation.

**c) No robots.txt, sitemap.xml, or RSS** — all four SEO endpoints 404 on the live site. No `og:image` or canonical URL either. For a blog, RSS is a real miss.

The idiomatic TanStack Start answer covers all three:

```ts
tanstackStart({
  srcDirectory: "src",
  prerender: { enabled: true, crawlLinks: true, failOnError: true },
})
```

Static HTML at build time, no round-trip, and once routes are prerendered a sitemap/RSS server route is trivial to add.

**Also from the Bun migration:** your Dockerfile runs `bun ./.output/server/index.mjs`, but the build log shows `preset: node-server`. The Bun path wants `nitro({ preset: 'bun' })`. It works today, but you're not getting what you migrated for.

---

## P2 — Replace, don't upgrade

### gray-matter → anything modern

`gray-matter@4.0.3` (last published 2019) depends on `js-yaml@3`, which depends on **esprima** — a full JavaScript parser. From your build output:

```
_libs/esprima.mjs              218.47 kB
_libs/gray-matter+[...].mjs    106.80 kB
```

**325 kB of server bundle** to parse frontmatter that looks like this:

```yaml
share: true
slug: thoughts_on_module_federation_2.0
title: Thoughts on Module Federation 2.0
date: 2025-10-13
tags:
  - module federation
```

This is server-only, so it costs you image size and cold start, not user bytes — but it's the single most disproportionate thing in the dependency tree. Swap in `yaml` (eemeli) with a ~10-line splitter, and both chunks vanish.

### The `[ACTIONS: {...}]` regex is the old way to do this

`ai.functions.ts:147` asks the model to emit JSON inside a bracketed tag, then regex-extracts it. AI SDK 7 does this natively — `generateText` accepts an `output` schema (Zod/Valibot/JSON Schema) so the model returns typed structured data directly, no string parsing, no `normalizeActions` defensive layer. If you want the palette to feel live, `streamText` supports the same thing.

### Delete `sanitizeHtml`

`src/utils/markdown.ts:9` is a blocklist regex sanitizer — the category of thing that is reliably bypassable. Every input is a markdown file you wrote, committed to `src/blogs/`. **It provides no security, only the appearance of it.** Delete it. (If you ever plan to accept markdown you didn't write, that's when you reach for a real parser-based sanitizer — but don't keep this in the meantime as a placeholder.)

---

## P3 — Cheap, verified wins

I actually ran these, so the numbers are real:

- **`"strict": true` in tsconfig: zero errors.** You currently only set `strictNullChecks`. Free. Adding `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` too gives 8 errors — but 4 are in `MatrixRain.tsx`, which is dead code (see below), so it's realistically a 4-fix change.
- **`define: { global: "globalThis" }` is vestigial.** I removed it, ran a full build and the test suite — both pass. (Reverted; your tree is clean.) It's a legacy CJS shim doing blind string replacement.
- **Unused runtime dependencies:** `isbot` and `web-vitals` are in `dependencies` and imported nowhere. `baseline-browser-mapping` in devDeps likewise.
- **Dead code:** `src/constants/sentry.tsx` (a hardcoded Sentry DSN, never imported), `src/components/effects/index.ts` and `src/components/Card/index.tsx` (barrel files nothing imports — everything imports directly), `MatrixRain.tsx` (only reachable through the dead barrel), and `_isLoaded` in `routes/index.tsx:13` (set, never read).
- **Two lockfiles:** `bun.lock` and `package-lock.json`. `packageManager` says npm and the Dockerfile runs `npm ci` — `bun.lock` is a stale artifact that will drift.
- **`routes/index.tsx:16`** attaches a `mousemove` listener that calls `setMousePosition` on every event, re-rendering the entire homepage continuously while the mouse moves. A CSS custom property written through a ref does the same parallax with zero re-renders.
- **`CommandAgent.tsx:118`** mutates a ref during render (`chatHistoryRef.current = chatHistory`). React Compiler is enabled on this project and that's explicitly disallowed — and it's unnecessary, since `sendAIQuery` already has the value.
- **`CommandAgent` modal** has no `role="dialog"`, no `aria-modal`, and no focus trap; the backdrop is a full-screen `<button>` sitting in the tab order. Native `<dialog>` with `showModal()` gives you all of that for free.
- **CI:** `superfly/flyctl-actions/setup-flyctl@master` is pinned to a moving branch — pin a tag or SHA. `actions/checkout@v4` → v5.
- **Node version tells three stories:** `@types/node ^26`, `engines.node >=22.12.0`, Dockerfile `NODE_VERSION=24` — and the actual runtime is Bun 1.4, not Node. `@types/node@26` will happily type APIs that don't exist where this runs.

I'd skip syntax highlighting (Shiki) for now — you have exactly one code block across two posts.

---

## One question

Your posts have exactly two code blocks but a lot of chrome. Separately: my saved note says your design direction as of July 2026 is "refined dark minimal, single cyan accent, no cyberpunk effects" — but the code is maximum cyberpunk (`#bf00ff`, `#ff0080`, MatrixRain, scan lines, `END_OF_TRANSMISSION`, and an AI system prompt that instructs a "cyberpunk/hacker personality"). Is that note stale, or is the redesign still pending? I didn't act on it either way.

---

Want me to start with P0? Both are small — the Groq model is a one-string change plus a label, and the vitest pin is three version numbers — and together they get your deploys green and your AI palette working again.

**Sources:**
- [Groq Model Deprecations](https://console.groq.com/docs/deprecations)
- [Groq Supported Models](https://console.groq.com/docs/models)
- [AI SDK Core: Generating Structured Data](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/ai-sdk-core/generating-structured-data)
- [AI SDK Core: Tool Calling](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/ai-sdk-core/tools-and-tool-calling)
- [Shiki](https://shiki.style/guide/)

## Bun.markdown API Overview

Bun includes a fast, built-in Markdown parser written in Rust that supports GitHub Flavored Markdown (GFM) extensions and provides three APIs: Bun.markdown.html() — render Markdown to an HTML string · Bun.markdown.render() — render Markdown with custom callbacks for each element · Bun.markdown.react() — render Markdown to React JSX elements.

## GFM Support

GitHub Flavored Markdown (GFM) extensions are enabled by default, including tables, strikethrough (~~text~~), task lists (- [x] done), and permissive autolinks. Additional options available include wikiLinks, latexMath, headingIds, and autolinkHeadings.

## Frontmatter Support

The native implementation includes YAML frontmatter extraction as export const frontmatter = {...}, which is built into the native markdown support.

## API Status

The Bun.markdown API is currently marked as unstable in the official Bun documentation. The interface works today, but specific options and method signatures may change in future Bun releases.

## Historical Note

Bun 1.3.8 (released January 2026) ships a built-in Markdown parser that replaces that entire chain with a single API call — no installs, no imports, no plugin configuration required.

input.prompt: Give full detail on the Bun.markdown API: all methods (html, render, react), all options, frontmatter/YAML frontmatter support and how it is accessed, GFM options, how raw/inline HTML is handled (escaped or passed through?), whether there is a sanitize or allowHtml option, syntax highlighting support, and any stability/unstable warnings. content.content:
# Bun.markdown API Overview

## Methods

Bun provides three markdown rendering APIs:

1. **`Bun.markdown.html()`** - Converts markdown strings to HTML output
2. **`Bun.markdown.render()`** - Parses markdown with custom JavaScript callbacks for element-level control
3. **`Bun.markdown.react()`** - Renders markdown directly as React elements/fragments

## Key Options

The parser supports these configurations:
- **GFM extensions**: tables, strikethrough, tasklists (all enabled by default)
- **Autolinks**: URL, WWW, and email detection (disabled by default)
- **Heading IDs**: Generate anchor IDs and autolink headings
- **Additional**: wiki links, underline support, LaTeX math, whitespace collapsing, HTML block/span control

## HTML Handling

The documentation specifies a `tagFilter` option for "GFM tag filter for disallowed HTML tags." Raw HTML blocks and inline HTML can be disabled via `noHtmlBlocks` and `noHtmlSpans` options, but there's no explicit "sanitize" option documented. HTML appears to pass through by default when enabled.

## Syntax Highlighting

No built-in syntax highlighting is provided. The `code` callback receives a `language` metadata parameter, allowing developers to implement external highlighting libraries.

## Frontmatter/YAML

The documentation contains **no mention** of frontmatter or YAML frontmatter support.

## Stability Status

The API carries an **"Unstable API" warning**: "This API is under active development and may change in future versions of Bun."

## Version Information

No specific Bun version introduction date is documented in this content.

## Bun.markdown API Status

The Bun.markdown API is currently marked as unstable in the official Bun documentation. Bun 1.3.8 (released January 2026) ships a built-in Markdown parser that replaces that entire chain with a single API call — no installs, no imports, no plugin configuration required.

## Replacing Dependencies

It adds native APIs that replace sharp, puppeteer, marked, json5, node-pty, node-cron and concurrently, and passes ~1,400 more Node.js tests. This indicates that Bun.markdown is designed to replace the `marked` library, though the search results don't specifically mention `gray-matter` as one of the dependencies being replaced.

## Implementation Details

A new Bun.markdown API uses a fast, CommonMark-compliant parser written in Zig (a port of md4c). Markdown can be rendered three ways: HTML output, callback-driven rendering (including stripping or custom formatting), and React elements; GitHub Flavored Markdown extensions are enabled by default, including tables, strikethrough, task lists, and permissive autolinks, with optional features like heading IDs, wiki links, and LaTeX math.

## Production Considerations

The API is still marked unstable, so pin your Bun version and verify output before deploying to production.

Module Federation 1.0 was groundbreaking for a few key reasons: it enabled different applications to pull in shared modules directly at runtime, making it possible to develop isolated micro-frontends while sharing dependencies across the board. In Module Federation 1.0, the Runtime was tightly coupled to Webpack, which made sense at the time, but limited flexibility when using other build tools. input.prompt: Describe the Bun.YAML API: parse and stringify. Is it marked as unstable or experimental? What Bun version introduced it?

content.content:
# Bun.YAML API Overview

The Bun.YAML namespace provides two core functions for YAML processing:

**parse()**: Converts YAML strings into JavaScript values. The documentation notes that "Every alias (`*name`) of an anchored collection yields the same object, and an alias may refer to a collection that contains it, so the result can be cyclic."

**stringify()**: Transforms JavaScript values into YAML format. It intelligently handles quoting and supports both flow-style (single-line) and block-style (multi-line) output through optional spacing parameters. The API can automatically infer anchors and aliases to handle circular references.

## Stability Status

The documentation provided does not explicitly mark these APIs as unstable or experimental. They appear to be stable, production-ready features.

## Version Information

The page header indicates this documentation corresponds to "Bun v1.4.0," but the content does not specify which version initially introduced the YAML API. The reference does not provide historical version information about when this feature was first added.

content.text: Yes — that changes my P2 conclusion substantially. And it turns out you already knew this: you shipped `Bun.markdown` once and backed it out. **P0 and P1 are unchanged.** The Groq shutdown and the red CI are untouched by any of this, and the `/blog` payload finding is orthogonal to which parser runs. Details below on why I'm confident about that last part. ## The history decides this `37d11cb` added `Bun.markdown.html`. Then `0168c29` — "Switch runtime from Bun to Node" — removed it, and your own commit message says why: > remove […] the `Bun.markdown.html` call in `src/utils/markdown.ts` (replaced with `marked` […]). **This lets the jsdom test shim in `setupTests.ts` go away entirely.** Then PR #181 moved the runtime back to Bun 1.4 — without restoring the markdown code. So the precondition that forced the revert is **half** gone. Precisely which half: **Gone:** production runs Bun (`CMD [ "bun", "./.output/server/index.mjs" ]`), and I confirmed parsing happens at *runtime*, not build time — `.output/server/_ssr/blogData-*.mjs` imports both `gray-matter` and `marked`. Bun's APIs are available exactly where the work happens. **Still there:** `vp test` runs Vitest under Node (I checked `--pool` — forks/threads/vmThreads, no Bun option), and `vp build` runs under vite-plus's managed Node. `src/__tests__/markdown.test.ts` cannot call `Bun.markdown`. Same wall as April. ## What I verified with Bun 1.4.0 locally **`Bun.YAML.parse` handles your frontmatter exactly.** I didn't know this existed when I wrote the first review — ignore my "swap gray-matter for the `yaml` package" suggestion, this is strictly better. It parsed all six of your frontmatter keys correctly, and it returns `date` as the string `"2025-10-13"` rather than a `Date` — so the `processedData.date instanceof Date` workaround at `markdown.ts:36-38` just disappears. **`Bun.markdown.html` output is equivalent to marked's.** I rendered both of your actual posts through both parsers and diffed. Across ~19KB of HTML, the *only* differences are: - `'` vs a literal `'` (both valid — apostrophes in text content need no escaping) - `` vs `` Zero structural differences. Code fences render identically, including `class="language-javascript"`. This is a genuine drop-in. **Together they delete ~378 kB of server bundle and two runtime dependencies:** `esprima.mjs` (218 kB) + `gray-matter+[…].mjs` (107 kB) + `marked.mjs` (53 kB) → nothing. Note this is *not* something Bun advertises: their 1.3.8 post lists `marked` as replaced, but gray-matter isn't mentioned — `Bun.YAML` is a separate API that happens to close the other half. ## The bonus: your sanitizer question gets a real answer I probed the HTML options: ``` {} → (passes through) {tagFilter: true} → <script>… but kept (GFM filter, partial) {noHtmlBlocks: true, noHtmlSpans: true} → <script>… <b>… (all escaped) ``` That's **parser-level** escaping. It upgrades my earlier advice from "delete the regex sanitizer, it protects nothing" to "delete it *and* get an actual guarantee for free." One constraint to accept knowingly: with those flags, any intentional inline HTML in a future post gets escaped as text. Neither current post has any, so it's the right default — but it does constrain how you write. ## What it costs — one named cost, and my recommendation **The test file.** `markdown.test.ts` has to run somewhere Bun exists. My recommendation: add a separate `"test:bun": "bun test src/__tests__/markdown.test.ts"` script and run it in CI alongside `vp test run`. Two runners is mild friction, but it exercises the real API. Do **not** shim `Bun` in `setupTests.ts`. A shim that reimplements the parsing means the test no longer tests what production runs — that's worse than no test, and it's the exact thing you already tried and abandoned. **Two caveats worth writing down:** - Bun's docs label `Bun.markdown` **unstable** — "under active development and may change in future versions." (`Bun.YAML` carries no such warning; I checked its reference page separately rather than assuming it inherits.) Your Dockerfile has `ARG BUN_VERSION=1.4`, a floating minor. **Pinning to a patch is a prerequisite for this swap, not a nice-to-have.** - `bun-types` went out in that same revert commit, and `env.d.ts` references only `node` and `vite/client`. `@types/bun` comes back as a devDep, and it can conflict with `@types/node` — watch that, given you already have three different Node-version stories in the repo. ## The prerender interaction — I tested it, there isn't one I wondered whether static prerendering would make this moot by moving parsing to build time. It doesn't. I added `prerender: { enabled: true, crawlLinks: true }` and built: - It works out of the box — 8 pages, both posts auto-discovered via crawling. - **The markdown deps stay in the server output:** `esprima.mjs`, `gray-matter+[…].mjs`, and `marked.mjs` are all still in `.output/server/_libs/` afterward. - **The payload bloat survives too:** prerendered `/blog/index.html` is still 46,082 bytes with 30,005 (65%) of hydration payload containing both posts' full HTML. Prerendering bakes the bloat into the static file rather than fixing it. So all three are independent levers, and you can take them in any order: the DTO fix for the payload, the Bun swap for the server bundle, prerendering for the round-trip and static hosting. (Config reverted; your tree is clean.) I'd still do P0 first — the Groq model and the vitest pin get your deploys green and the AI palette working again, and they're maybe five lines between them. Want me to start there, or go straight at the Bun markdown swap? **Sources:** - [Bun Docs — Markdown](https://bun.com/docs/runtime/markdown) - [Bun API Reference — Bun.YAML](https://bun.com/reference/bun/YAML) - [Bun v1.3.8 release notes](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.3.8) - [Groq Model Deprecations](https://console.groq.com/docs/deprecations)

content.text: Everything is done except the Bun markdown swap. Let me check my conclusion on that before reporting.

All 33 items are resolved — 29 shipped, 4 deliberately not. `vp check` is clean, tests pass, coverage gates for real, and the build prerenders 8 pages.

## Shipped

**P0 — main is unblocked.** Model moved to `openai/gpt-oss-20b` behind a new `src/constants/ai.ts` (the palette footer reads from the same constant, so it can't drift again). The silent catch now logs the real cause and surfaces it. Vitest/coverage-v8 pinned to `4.1.10` in all three places — `vp test run --coverage` runs again, which was the exact CI step failing.

**P1.** `/blog` now loads `getAllBlogPostSummaries()` — verified live: **46,082 → 31,449 bytes, zero `html:` fields in the payload**. Coverage thresholds moved to Vitest 4's top-level form. Docker pinned to `BUN_VERSION=1.4.0`.

**P3.** `strict: true` (zero errors, as measured). Deleted the `global` define shim, `isbot`, `web-vitals`, `baseline-browser-mapping`, `bun.lock`, `sentry.tsx`, both barrel files, `MatrixRain`, `BlogCard`, `ScrambleText`/`Typewriter`, and — after checking — `ToolCard`, which turned out to be pre-redesign markup that `tool.tsx` doesn't use. Parallax now writes rAF-throttled CSS custom properties through a ref (and respects `prefers-reduced-motion`) instead of re-rendering the homepage on every pointer move. The render-phase ref mutation in `CommandAgent` is gone.

**P4.** Prerendering enabled — 8 pages, both posts auto-crawled. `robots.txt`, `sitemap.xml`, and `rss.xml` as server routes (all three verified serving 200 with correct content). Canonical + og:url + og:image + Twitter card on every route via a `pageMeta` helper — and `/`, `/tool`, and `/reading-list` had **no `head()` at all**, so they were inheriting the generic root title; they have real titles now. Generated a 1200×630 og:image matching the site. AI handler now uses `Output.object` with a zod schema instead of the `[ACTIONS: …]` regex.

## Where I deviated from the table

- **#6 — kept, not dropped.** `node_modules/vite` *is* `@voidzero-dev/vite-plus-core` via that alias, consumed by `@rolldown/plugin-babel` and `@tailwindcss/vite`. Removing it would break the build. I realigned 0.2.8 → 0.2.9 instead.
- **#9 — reverted, traded for #30.** `nitro({ preset: "bun" })` breaks prerendering (`UND_ERR_HEADERS_TIMEOUT`, 0 pages) because the prerenderer boots the built server under Node. Since node-server output runs fine under Bun — I verified all 8 routes serve 200 under `bun ./.output/server/index.mjs` — I kept prerender and left a comment in `vite.config.ts` explaining why the preset isn't set.
- **#28** — `setup-flyctl@v1.5` doesn't exist (used `1.6`); checkout is on **v7**, not the v5 I listed.
- **#29** — `@types/node` went `^26` → `^24.10.1`. That's a deliberate *downgrade* to match the runtime.
- **#7** — thresholds are 80/60/90/90 against actuals of 91.8/70.6/100/97.7. Calibrated to reality rather than the aspirational 70-across-the-board that was never enforcing anything. I added two tests for the summary DTO rather than lower the function threshold.

## The dialog rewrite — worth reading

`<dialog>` + `showModal()` gives a real focus trap and inert background. Getting there surfaced a non-obvious bug: **neither React's synthetic `onCancel` nor `onClose` fires for `<dialog>` here**, and on the Escape path the native `close` event doesn't fire either — only `cancel` does. My first two attempts left `isOpen` stuck at `true`, so after Escape the next Cmd+K silently did nothing. It's now a native `cancel` listener that preventDefaults and lets React drive the single close path. Verified on a clean load: opens modal with focus on the input, Escape closes, **Cmd+K reopens on the first press**, backdrop dismisses, toggle works.

(Two testing notes: the automation harness swallows Escape entirely — `keysSeen: []` — so I used `requestClose()`, which fires the identical path. And several intermediate runs were contaminated by state left over from the previous run; the passing result above is from a fresh page load.)

## What I did not do — #11–16, the Bun markdown swap

Two independent blockers, one of which I created by shipping #30:

1. `import.meta.glob` doesn't exist in Bun (verified), so `blogData.ts` can't run under `bun test`. The swap needs either a stub parser — which I told you is worse than no test, and is what `0168c29` already tried — or a Vite-plugin re-architecture you didn't approve.
2. **Prerendering requires the Node build path.** The prerenderer runs loaders under Node, so a Bun-only `markdown.ts` would break the 8 pages I just prerendered. Same conflict as #9 vs #30.

So it's mutually exclusive with prerendering, not a preference call. The one genuinely valuable piece — **#13, deleting the regex `sanitizeHtml`** — is separable and still available under marked; I left it in place because removing it also means rewriting `markdown.test.ts:60-73`, which asserts *removal* where marked passes raw HTML through. Say the word and I'll do that one on its own.

## Two things I could not verify

No `GROQ_API_KEY` locally and no Fly access, so:

- The `openai/gpt-oss-20b` call has **never actually hit Groq**. The id is in the SDK's type union and on Groq's model list, and the palette round-trips to the server function correctly — but the generation itself is untested.
- `Output.object` with the zod schema is **entirely unexercised**. Whether gpt-oss-20b honors json_schema through `@ai-sdk/groq` is unknown; if it doesn't, `generateText` throws and the improved catch surfaces it — graceful failure, not a working feature.

Both ride in the same deploy. **Smoke-test the command palette once it's up** — if the AI is still broken, that's where to look.

Also: `SITE_URL` defaults to `https://xiaofeng-blog.fly.dev` since `xiaofeng.dev` belongs to a different person. Override with `VITE_SITE_URL` at build time or `SITE_URL` at runtime if you have another domain.

Nothing is committed — 588 insertions, 2,187 deletions across 27 files plus 6 new ones. And I still haven't touched the cyberpunk/minimal design question; that memory may be stale, and it'd change what's worth doing in `tailwind.css`.

- The test now asserts escaping rather than stripping, plus a new test that markdown-authored links still render as real `<a>` tags
- One assertion I wrote was too crude — `not.toContain("onclick=")` failed because the *escaped* text legitimately contains `onclick="`. Tightened to `onclick="`, which distinguishes a live attribute from inert text.
- 16 tests pass, coverage 92.5/69.4/100/97.8 (all above the gate), `vp check` clean, build prerenders 8 pages

That closes out all 33 items: 30 shipped, 3 not (#11, #12, #14 — the Bun parser swap, blocked by the `import.meta.glob` test seam and the prerender conflict).
